analogy.p: A wired connection is like a water pipe running straight from the tap to the sink: the water (data) goes where the pipe goes, keeps its pressure (speed), and nobody else can drink from it unless they tap the pipe. Fibre is a wide, modern main pipe that can carry much more water over long distances. A wireless connection is like using a megaphone in a classroom: everyone in range can hear it, it is easy to move around, but the further away you are or the more walls in the way, the harder it is to hear, and many people talking at once drown each other out. The analogy breaks down because radio waves are not simply 'louder or quieter'; Wi-Fi uses encryption so only authorised devices can decode the message.

bullets: Describe **wired** connections: **Ethernet** over copper cable (twisted pair) and **fibre-optic** cable.
Describe **wireless** connections: **Wi-Fi** (radio waves to a WAP) and **Bluetooth** (short-range, low-power connection between nearby devices).
Compare wired and wireless on **speed, reliability, security, range, cost, mobility, installation and interference**.
Link the connection type to the **hardware** needed (NIC, switch, router, WAP).
**Choose and justify** the best connection for a scenario, often recommending a mix of both.
Use correct terms: **transmission media**, **bandwidth**, **latency**, **interference**, **encryption**.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: OCR J277 section 1.3 expects you to understand how devices are connected into a network using **wired** and **wireless** connections. You should know the main transmission media (copper cable, fibre-optic cable and radio waves), the standards **Ethernet**, **Wi-Fi** and **Bluetooth**, and be able to compare wired and wireless connections for a given scenario. Questions are usually 'give two advantages/disadvantages', 'compare' or 'recommend and justify', so the skill is matching features to a situation.

bullets: **Copper cable** carries data as **electrical signals**; the most common type is Ethernet **twisted pair**.
**Fibre-optic cable** carries data as **pulses of light** along thin glass or plastic strands.
**Wireless** uses **radio waves** (Wi-Fi) or other short-range radio (Bluetooth) through the air, with no cable.
The signal gets weaker over distance (**attenuation**) and can be disturbed by **interference**, which limits how far each medium can go.
The **NIC** in each device converts data into the right kind of signal for the medium.
Wired media are a **guided** path (the cable); wireless is **unguided** (anyone in range can receive it).
core.h: Transmission media: the path the data travels along
core.p: **Transmission media** are the physical paths that carry data between devices. Data is always converted into a signal that suits the medium: electrical pulses in copper cable, pulses of light in fibre-optic cable, and radio waves through the air for wireless. The choice of medium affects the speed, distance, cost, reliability and security of the connection, so almost every comparison question comes back to these properties.

bullets: Common cable types are **Cat5e** and **Cat6** twisted-pair cable; a single run is limited to about **100 metres** before the signal must be boosted.
Each device has its own cable to a **switch**, so devices do not compete for the same radio space.
Wired connections are **fast and reliable**, with consistent speed and low **latency**, which suits servers, desktop PCs and video work.
They are **more secure**, because someone must have physical access to plug in; there is no signal leaking through walls.
They are **not affected by walls or other Wi-Fi networks**, though copper can suffer electrical **interference** from nearby equipment.
Disadvantages: **cables must be installed**, devices cannot easily move, and cables can be a trip hazard and add cost.
Adding more devices usually means **more cable and more switch ports**.
core.h: Wired connections: Ethernet over copper cable
core.p: **Ethernet** is the standard used for most wired LANs. Devices are connected by cables with **RJ45** plugs into the Ethernet ports of a switch or router, in a star layout. The cables contain pairs of copper wires that are **twisted** together, which helps reduce interference between the pairs. Modern Ethernet commonly gives speeds of 1 gigabit per second (Gbit/s) or more, and because the cable is a dedicated path, the connection is fast, stable and low delay.

bullets: Light travels extremely fast and carries a **very large amount of data**, so fibre provides very high **bandwidth** and speed.
Fibre can run for **many kilometres** without the signal fading much, far further than copper.
It is **not affected by electrical interference**, because it carries light and not electricity.
It is harder to tap without being noticed, so it is generally **more secure** than copper.
Disadvantages: the cable and the equipment at each end are **more expensive**, and the cable is **more fragile** and harder to install and repair.
Typical uses: the **internet backbone**, links between buildings or between a school's floors, and broadband to homes ('full fibre').
core.p: **Fibre-optic cable** sends data as pulses of light along a very thin strand of glass (the core). The light stays inside the core because of the surrounding layer, called the **cladding**, so the signal can travel a long way with little loss. This makes fibre the best choice for very high speed and for long distances, such as the backbone of the internet, links between buildings and many broadband connections to homes.

bullets: **Signal**: copper = electrical; fibre = light.
**Speed/bandwidth**: fibre is higher than copper.
**Distance**: copper is about 100 m per run for Ethernet; fibre can be kilometres.
**Interference**: copper can be affected by electrical interference; fibre is not.
**Cost**: copper is cheaper; fibre is more expensive to buy and install.
**Robustness**: copper is tougher to handle; fibre is more delicate.
**Best use**: copper for ordinary room-to-room wiring; fibre for long distances and high-demand links such as between buildings.
core.p: Exam questions often ask you to choose between the two cable types. Remember that copper is cheaper and easier, fibre is faster, longer-range and free from electrical interference. Each time, decide what the scenario cares about most: cost, speed, distance or reliability.

bullets: A wireless NIC and a **WAP** (or wireless router) are needed for Wi-Fi.
Most Wi-Fi uses the **2.4 GHz** and **5 GHz** radio bands; 2.4 GHz usually has a longer range but is slower and more crowded, whereas 5 GHz is usually faster but has a shorter range.
**Advantages**: no cables to install, users can **move around** (mobility), easy to add new devices, and can reach places where cabling is difficult.
**Disadvantages**: usually **slower and less stable** than wired, signal **weakens with distance** and is blocked by walls, floors and metal.
**Interference** from other Wi-Fi networks, microwaves and Bluetooth devices can reduce speed.
All devices on one WAP **share the bandwidth**, so performance drops as more users connect.
**Security risk**: the signal can be picked up by anyone in range, so networks need **encryption** (WPA2/WPA3), a strong password, and often a hidden or separate guest network.
Typical range is **tens of metres** indoors, shorter with thick walls.
core.p: **Wi-Fi** is the wireless networking standard that lets devices join a LAN using **radio waves** instead of cables. A device with a wireless NIC communicates with a **wireless access point (WAP)** or wireless router, which is wired into the rest of the network. Wi-Fi is hugely popular because it lets laptops, phones, tablets and smart devices connect from anywhere in range, but the shared radio signal has limits that students must be able to describe.

bullets: Range is short, typically around **10 metres** for common devices.
It uses **low power**, so it suits small battery-powered devices.
Data rates are lower than Wi-Fi, which is fine for audio, mice, keyboards and small file transfers.
Devices must be **paired** (they recognise each other, often with a code) before they exchange data.
It uses the same **2.4 GHz** band as some Wi-Fi, so the two can interfere slightly.
Exam contrast: **Wi-Fi** = connects devices to a **network and the internet**, longer range, higher speed; **Bluetooth** = connects **two nearby devices** directly, short range, low power.
core.p: **Bluetooth** is a wireless technology designed for **short-range, low-power** connections between nearby devices, such as a phone and headphones, a keyboard and a computer, or a smartwatch and a phone. Devices must be **paired** first. Bluetooth creates small personal networks rather than connecting to a LAN or the internet, so it is not a replacement for Wi-Fi.

bullets: **Speed**: wired is generally faster; wireless speeds fall with distance and obstacles.
**Reliability**: wired is more stable; wireless can drop out because of interference or weak signal.
**Security**: wired is more secure (physical access needed); wireless can be intercepted, so it needs encryption.
**Mobility**: wireless allows movement; wired ties devices to a socket.
**Cost/installation**: wired needs cable, trunking and sockets; wireless needs a few WAPs, so is often cheaper and quicker for the building, though wired devices can be cheaper to run.
**Range/coverage**: wired reaches wherever the cable is laid; wireless is limited by signal range.
**Interference**: wired copper has little; wireless has a lot.
**Number of devices**: wired devices have their own cable; wireless devices share the airtime.
core.h: Wired v wireless: the full comparison
core.p: This is the most examined idea in the topic. Instead of memorising a list, understand why each difference exists. Cables give a dedicated, protected path, so wired is faster, more stable and more secure. Radio waves spread through the air for anyone nearby, so wireless is more convenient but shared, weaker and easier to intercept.

bullets: **Servers, video editing, game consoles, fixed desktops**: **wired** for speed, stability and security.
**Laptops, tablets and phones used around a site, visitors**: **wireless** (Wi-Fi) for mobility and convenience.
**Connecting buildings across a site or very long distances**: **fibre**.
**Historic or hard-to-wire building**: **wireless**, because installing cable would be costly or not allowed.
**Sensitive data**: **wired** where possible, plus encryption and passwords on any wireless.
**Headphones, mouse, keyboard**: **Bluetooth**.
A balanced conclusion such as 'wired to the main devices and Wi-Fi for staff laptops' shows evaluation.
core.h: Choosing between wired and wireless in a scenario
core.p: The skill that earns top marks is applying the comparison to the details in the question. Underline the clues (mobile users, large data transfers, security needs, a historic building where drilling is not allowed) and match them to the strengths of each connection. In many realistic scenarios the best answer is a **mixture**: wired for fixed or demanding devices, wireless for mobile or guest users.

bullets: **Distance** from the WAP: the further away, the weaker the signal and the slower the connection.
**Obstacles** such as thick walls, floors and metal block or weaken the signal.
**Interference** from neighbouring networks, microwave ovens and other devices.
**Number of users**: all devices share the WAP's bandwidth, so more users means less each.
**Fixes**: move or add WAPs, use the 5 GHz band for speed at short range, reduce the number of users per WAP, or use a cable for demanding devices.
**Bandwidth** is the amount of data per second the connection can carry; **latency** is the delay.
Wired connections avoid most of these problems.
core.p: Because radio waves are shared and can be blocked, wireless speed varies from place to place. Examiners often ask why a Wi-Fi connection is slow, so you should be able to list the causes and the fix for each. This is also a data-interpretation skill: if speed falls as you move away from the WAP, the cause is signal weakening with distance.

bullets: **Encryption (WPA2 or WPA3)** scrambles the data so intercepted signals cannot be read without the key.
A **strong password** (key) prevents unauthorised devices joining.
A separate **guest network** keeps visitors away from internal systems.
**MAC address filtering** allows only listed devices (though it is not perfect).
A **firewall** on the router controls traffic entering and leaving the network.
Wired networks are inherently harder to intercept but should still be protected from physical access and unauthorised plugging-in.
core.p: A wireless signal passes through walls, so people outside the building could try to use it or read it. Therefore wireless networks need protection. These ideas link to the network security topic and often appear in 'explain how' questions.

bullets: **Network hardware**: wired devices connect to a **switch**; wireless devices connect to a **WAP**; both reach the internet through a **router**; every device needs a **NIC** (wired or wireless).
**Topologies**: wired star networks use cables to a central switch; wireless networks are effectively a star around the WAP; mesh networks may use wireless links.
**Protocols and layers**: the same protocols (TCP/IP, HTTP) run over wired or wireless links; the medium is the lowest layer.
**Network security**: encryption and passwords matter more for wireless.
**Mobile and IoT devices**: rely on Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, which is why those technologies matter in everyday life.
**Bandwidth and data transfer**: video streaming and cloud storage need high bandwidth, favouring fibre and wired connections.
core.p: This topic connects to hardware, topologies and security. A strong answer will name the right device and say how the connection type affects performance. Examiners also like to see you say why a protocol or security measure works over either kind of medium, because that shows you understand the layers of a network rather than a list of facts.

bullets: The device's **wireless NIC** detects nearby networks, each identified by a network name (**SSID**).
The user selects the network and enters the **password** (security key), which sets up the **encryption** (for example WPA2 or WPA3).
The **WAP** (often built into the router) receives the radio signal and passes the data on to the wired network or the internet.
Data sent over the air is **encrypted**, so anyone who intercepts the radio waves cannot read it without the key.
**Bluetooth** devices are linked by **pairing**: the two devices find each other and agree a connection, usually with a code or confirmation.
Wireless devices **share** the radio waves, so more devices at once means less speed for each.
Wired devices need only plug the **RJ45** cable into the NIC port and the switch or router, with no password needed to join (but physical access is).
In an exam, put the steps in the order they happen and name each device.
core.h: Setting up a wireless connection step by step
core.p: A wireless connection needs both ends to agree how to talk before any data is sent, and exam answers that describe the steps in order show real understanding. A device has a wireless network interface card (NIC) that can send and receive radio signals, and the wireless access point (WAP) is the device that the network is built around. Security is part of the set-up because radio waves pass through walls, so the data is encrypted before it is sent.

exam: **Give/State two advantages of wired (2 marks)**: e.g. 'faster/more stable' and 'more secure'. Each must be a different idea.
**Compare** questions need **both sides in one sentence**: 'Wired is faster than wireless because it does not share airtime' scores; two separate lists do not.
Always **use the scenario**: 'because the staff use laptops around the building, Wi-Fi is suitable' earns the application mark.
For **recommend/justify (4 marks)**: state the connection, give a reason, give a second reason or detail, and mention a drawback or a mix of both.
**6-mark discuss**: cover speed, reliability, security, cost, mobility and installation, then give a reasoned conclusion that fits the scenario.
Use precise terms: **interference, bandwidth, signal strength, encryption, mobility, latency**; avoid 'it is better' or 'it is quicker' alone.
Say **why**: wireless is slower **because the signal is shared and weakened by distance and walls**.
Name hardware needed: **wireless NIC and WAP** for Wi-Fi; **switch and cables** for Ethernet.
For Bluetooth: mention **short range, low power, pairing**, and a typical use such as headphones or a keyboard.
Know a **drawback for every advantage**; examiners often ask 'give one disadvantage' for the option you recommended.
Graph/data tips: if speed drops as distance from a WAP increases, link it to **signal weakening**; if it drops when more devices connect, link it to **shared bandwidth**.
**Order the steps (2 to 3 marks)**: for joining a Wi-Fi network write NIC finds the network, user selects it and enters the password, data is encrypted, WAP passes data on.

mistakes.r: Wireless is more **convenient**, but wired is usually **faster, more reliable and more secure**; judge by the scenario.
mistakes.w: Wireless is always better because it is modern.

mistakes.r: Wi-Fi is a way of **connecting a device to a network**; the internet is a worldwide network of networks.
mistakes.w: Wi-Fi and the internet are the same thing.

mistakes.r: Wired is **more secure** because physical access is needed, but data can still be attacked through the network; say 'more secure', not 'completely secure'.
mistakes.w: Wired connections have no security risks.

mistakes.r: Fibre is faster because it carries **pulses of light**, which allow very high bandwidth and low loss over long distances.
mistakes.w: Fibre is faster because it is thicker.

mistakes.r: Bluetooth connects **nearby devices directly** over a short range; it is not used to access the internet by itself.
mistakes.w: Bluetooth connects you to the internet.

mistakes.r: Wireless can be **cheaper to install** (no cables), but may need several WAPs, encryption and can be slower; wired devices can be cheaper to run.
mistakes.w: Wireless is cheaper in every way.

mistakes.r: It still needs a **wireless NIC** in the device and a **WAP** or wireless router.
mistakes.w: A wireless connection does not need any hardware.

mistakes.r: Copper cables can suffer electrical interference too; **fibre** is the type not affected.
Fibre-optic cable carries data as **light**, and copper cable carries data as **electrical signals**; Wi-Fi uses radio waves.
mistakes.w: Saying that fibre-optic cable sends data as electricity or as radio waves.

summary: OCR J277 1.3 requires you to describe wired (Ethernet over copper and fibre-optic) and wireless (Wi-Fi and Bluetooth) connections, compare them on speed, reliability, security, range, cost and mobility, and recommend the best option for a scenario. It matters because Paper 1 regularly asks you to compare connection types and to justify a choice using details from the question.

terms.d: The physical paths, such as cable or radio waves, along which data is carried between devices.
A standard for wired networks in which devices are connected by cables (usually copper twisted pair) to a switch.
Copper cable in which pairs of wires are twisted together to reduce interference.
Cable that carries data as pulses of light along thin glass or plastic strands.
Wireless networking technology that connects devices to a network using radio waves via a wireless access point.
A short-range, low-power wireless technology used to connect nearby devices directly.
Wireless access point: allows wireless devices to connect to a wired network.
A network interface card with an antenna that sends and receives radio waves.
The amount of data that can be transferred in a given time, usually measured in bits per second.
The delay between sending data and it being received.
Unwanted signals that disturb or corrupt the wanted signal.
The weakening of a signal as it travels over distance.
Scrambling data so that it cannot be understood without the correct key.
Security standards that encrypt Wi-Fi traffic.
The ability to use a device while moving around, without being tied to a cable.
The process of linking two Bluetooth devices so they can exchange data.
The connector on the end of an Ethernet cable.
The name that identifies a wireless network, shown to devices that search for networks.
The range of radio frequencies a wireless technology uses; Wi-Fi and Bluetooth often share the 2.4 GHz band, which can cause interference.

worked.ans: Advantage: wired connections are usually faster and more stable because each device has its own cable and there is little interference (1). Advantage: wired connections are more secure because someone needs physical access to plug in (1). Disadvantage: devices cannot move around freely and cables must be installed, which costs time and money (1).
worked.q: Give two advantages and one disadvantage of a wired connection compared with a wireless connection. [3 marks]
steps: Choose a disadvantage such as mobility or installation.

worked.ans: The scanner should use a wired Ethernet connection because it sends very large files and needs a fast, stable, secure connection (1+1). The ward tablets should use Wi-Fi through WAPs because staff move between rooms and need mobility (1). Wi-Fi must be encrypted, because patient data is sensitive and wireless signals can be intercepted (1).
worked.q: A hospital wants to connect its offices, ward tablets and a scanner that sends very large files. Recommend a combination of connections and justify it. [4 marks]
steps: Add security or fibre for linking buildings.

worked.ans: Wi-Fi connects devices to a network and the internet through a WAP, whereas Bluetooth connects two nearby devices directly (1). Wi-Fi has a longer range, tens of metres, but Bluetooth is short range, about 10 metres (1). Wi-Fi gives higher data rates, while Bluetooth uses low power and a lower rate (1). Wi-Fi suits laptops and phones, whereas Bluetooth suits headphones and keyboards (1).
